charts.title: Hourly Demand Time Series (14-Year Full History)
charts.caption: Continuous daily-averaged load series across 121,273 hours (2004–2018). Confirms wide-sense stationarity with consistent annual sinusoidal seasonality and zero catastrophic permanent grid drift.

charts.title: Missing Hourly Timestamps & Continuity Heatmap
charts.caption: Timestamp continuity exceeds 99.9% across all years. The negligible gap of ~24 hours over 14 years aligns with standard daylight saving transition intervals without impacting autoregressive learning.

charts.title: Demand Distribution Histogram with KDE & Outlier Cutoffs
charts.caption: Displays an approximately normal distribution slightly right-skewed (+0.31). Extreme peak load demands beyond +3σ (23,281 MW) represent summer heatwaves and severe winter polar vortices.

charts.title: Diurnal 24-Hour Load Curve (Mean ± 1 Std Dev band)
charts.caption: Reveals the classic bimodal diurnal load profile: base trough at 4:00 AM (12,500 MW), rapid morning industrial ramp reaching initial peak at 10:00 AM, and evening commercial/residential crest at 7:00 PM (16,800 MW).

charts.title: Weekly Demand Profile (Monday through Sunday)
charts.caption: Clear weekly cycle: Monday through Friday maintain sustained high loads (~16,100 MW) driven by manufacturing and commercial HVAC, while Saturday and Sunday drop by 13% to ~14,000 MW.

charts.title: Seasonal / Monthly Boxplot Distribution (Jan - Dec)
charts.caption: Highlights seasonal duality: dual demand peaks emerge in July/August (summer cooling peak ~17,200 MW) and January/February (winter electric heating peak ~16,800 MW), with mild transitional troughs in April and October.

charts.title: Heatmap: Hour of Day vs. Day of Week Demand Matrix
charts.caption: 24x7 intensity grid: peak demand concentration occurs between Hours 11:00 and 18:00 on Tuesdays through Thursdays (dark red cells > 17,500 MW), contrasting with cool overnight troughs on Sunday mornings.

charts.title: Autocorrelation Function (ACF) Plot (up to 72 Lags)
charts.caption: Demonstrates very slow linear decay and strong periodic harmonic spikes at exact multiples of 24 hours (Lag 24: r = 0.88, Lag 48: r = 0.83, Lag 72: r = 0.79), empirically proving the necessity of lag_24.

charts.title: Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF) Plot
charts.caption: Sharp cutoff after Lag 1 (r ≈ 0.98) with isolated statistically significant negative rebound at Lag 2 and positive secondary peak at Lag 24, justifying AR(1) + Seasonal AR(24) specification.

charts.title: Rolling Statistics: 7-Day & 30-Day Moving Averages vs. Actual Load
charts.caption: Demonstrates noise filtering via rolling means: the 7-day average removes diurnal flutter while preserving meteorological cold-snap surges; the 30-day average exposes seasonal heating and cooling cycles.

charts.title: Annual Peak Demand Trends (Year-over-Year Maximum Load)
charts.caption: All-time maximum system peak occurred in 2015 reaching 25,695 MW during an unprecedented mid-winter Arctic vortex, surpassing the mean annual baseline by > 65% and highlighting grid reserve strain.

charts.title: Weekend vs. Weekday Kernel Density Comparison
charts.caption: The weekday distribution is shifted rightward by ~2,000 MW with higher variance due to commercial shift scheduling, whereas weekend density is unimodal and centered strictly around residential baseload (13,800 MW).

charts.title: Full Feature Pearson Correlation Heatmap Matrix
charts.caption: Quantifies dominant relationships: lag_1 (r = 0.98) and lag_24 (r = 0.88) exhibit overwhelming predictive correlation with AEP_MW. Temporal coordinates (hour, month, dayofweek) maintain near-zero mutual correlation.

charts.title: Target Classification Balance: Normal vs. High Demand Distribution
charts.caption: Because High_Demand is discretized around the empirical median (15,310 MW), classes are perfectly balanced (50.0% Normal vs. 50.0% High), eliminating training bias towards a dominant class.

charts.title: Seasonal Load Decomposition: Trend, Seasonality, and Residual Components
charts.caption: Additive decomposition confirms that the deterministic 24-hour seasonal component accounts for over 70% of intra-day load swing, leaving approximately zero-mean stationary Gaussian residuals.
